title: Foundations
subtitle: Start from zero
description: Your first real English: the structures every sentence uses, practised out loud in small conversations.

themes.title: Language-exchange café
themes.subtitle: Meet and greet
themes.situation: You are at a friendly language-exchange café. Meet the learner, exchange names, countries and jobs using the verb to be.

themes.title: Nice to meet you
themes.subtitle: Start somewhere small
themes.situation: Meet the learner for the first time. Learn their interests through natural introductions.

lessons.title: The verb “to be”
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself and ask simple questions with am/is/are.

explanation: Every English sentence needs a subject and a verb. The most important verb is “to be”. It tells you what someone is, how someone feels, or where something is.
One verb, three present forms. With I use am: “I am Ana.” With you, we and they use are: “You are my friend.” With he, she and it use is: “She is a doctor.”
In everyday talk, English shortens it: I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're. When you chat, say “I'm Ana”, not “I am Ana”.

examples.text: The café is near the station.

expressions.note: With your name, age or feeling: I'm Ana. I'm tired.
Never “I from …” — the am is obligatory.
Are you a student? Are you tired?

expressions.text: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
expressions.meaning: Short answers to an Are-you question.

expressions.note: He's a teacher — the a matters with professions.

expressions.meaning: The fixed phrase when you meet someone.

lessons.situation: You meet someone new at a friendly language-exchange café. Introduce yourselves and ask simple questions with the verb to be.

questions.prompt: Hello! I'm Ana. What's your name?
questions.watch: Answering only the name without the verb: accept it, then recast with “I'm …”.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
questions.watch: “I from Spain” — recast “I am FROM Spain”, stress am.

questions.prompt: Are you a student?
questions.watch: “Yes, I student” — the short answer needs am.

questions.prompt: How are you today?
questions.watch: “I fine” — recast “I'm fine”.

questions.prompt: Is your city big or small?
questions.watch: “My city big” — recast “My city IS big”.

questions.prompt: We're friends now! Where is your family from?
questions.watch: “My family from …” — recast with is.

lessons.title: Questions & negatives with “to be”
lessons.goal: Ask yes/no and wh- questions, and say what is not true, with am/is/are.

explanation: To ask a yes/no question, put the verb first. “You are tired.” becomes “Are you tired?” “She is a teacher.” becomes “Is she a teacher?”
To say something is not true, add not. “I am not late.” In talk we shorten: is not → isn't, are not → aren't. And I'm not is already short.
Real questions add question words: what, where, who, how. They go before the verb: “Where are you from?” Short forms: what's = what is, where's = where is.

expressions.note: Are you OK? Are you new here?

expressions.meaning: Say what is not true about you.
expressions.note: I'm not from Madrid — I'm from Seville.

expressions.meaning: Say what is not true about others.
expressions.note: She isn't here. They aren't at home.
Where's the station? Where are my keys?

lessons.situation: You chat with a new neighbour in the lift. Ask simple questions and say what is and isn't true for you.

questions.prompt: Hi! Are you new in the building?
expected: No, I'm not. I'm on the third floor.
questions.watch: “Yes, I new” — short answers repeat am.

questions.prompt: Is your flat big?
questions.watch: “No, it not big” — the negative is isn't.

questions.prompt: I'm Marta, by the way. What's your name?
questions.watch: “What you name?” — the question needs is: “What's your name?”.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
questions.watch: “Where you from?” — don't drop are.

questions.prompt: Are your neighbours friendly?
questions.watch: “Yes, they friendly” — repeat are.

questions.prompt: I'm not from this city — I'm from Valencia. And you?
questions.watch: “I no from …” — the negative is “I'm not from …”.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.goal: Give a complete self-introduction: name, age, country, nationality and job.

explanation: A good introduction answers five small questions: your name, your age, your country or city, your nationality, and your job.
In English, age and nationality use the verb to be. “I'm 30.” “I'm Mexican.” Say “I'm 30”, never “I have 30”.
With jobs we say a/an: “I'm a nurse.” “He's an engineer.” Nationality words are adjectives: from Spain → I'm Spanish; from Mexico → I'm Mexican.

expressions.meaning: Adjective with be: Spanish, Turkish, Brazilian.
Your job. Use an before a vowel sound.
The polite answer to “Nice to meet you”.
expressions.note: Same smile, one extra word: too.

lessons.situation: First day in class: the teacher asks everyone to stand up and introduce themselves to two classmates.

questions.prompt: Good morning! Please introduce yourself.
questions.watch: One line is fine — the tutor will ask for more.

questions.prompt: Lovely to meet you. How old are you?
questions.watch: “I have 25” — age uses be: “I'm 25”.

questions.prompt: Where are you from?
questions.watch: “I'm Spanish from Spain” — keep it simple: “I'm from …”.

questions.prompt: So you're from Italy — you're Italian, right?
questions.watch: “I'm Italy” — the country is Italy, the person is Italian.

questions.prompt: What's your job?
questions.watch: “I'm teacher” — jobs need a/an: “I'm a teacher”.

questions.prompt: Great! Now introduce your friend: this is Carlos.
questions.focus: talking about a third person with is
questions.watch: “Carlos is teacher” — add a: “a teacher”.

themes.title: Family photo album
themes.subtitle: Who's who
themes.situation: You show the learner a family photo album. Name the people, ask about each other's families and say who has what.

themes.title: The lost jumper
themes.subtitle: Whose is it?
themes.situation: A jumper appeared in the classroom. Help find its owner: ask what things are, whose they are and what they look like.

lessons.title: a/an, the & plurals
lessons.goal: Talk about one thing, a specific thing and many things.

explanation: Use a or an for one of many — any one. Use an before a vowel sound: a book, an apple, an hour.
Use the when the listener knows exactly which one. First we introduce with a/an (“I have a cat”), then we talk about it with the (“The cat is old”).
For more than one, most words take -s: book → books. After -s, -sh, -ch, -x we add -es: bus → buses, watch → watches. A few are special: person → people, child → children.

expressions.meaning: One of many; an before a vowel sound.
Special plurals: person → people, child → children.

lessons.situation: You help at a small shop on market day: count things, name things and ask for one specific item.

questions.prompt: Welcome! Can I help you?
questions.watch: The first time you name a thing: a/an, not the.

questions.prompt: This one here on the shelf? The blue one?
questions.watch: “Yes, blue one” — keep the: “the blue one”.

questions.prompt: How many bags do you need?
questions.watch: “two bag” — plural needs -s: “two bags”.

questions.prompt: Do you want apples or oranges?
questions.watch: “three orange” — add -s.

questions.prompt: The watches are over there. How many do you need?
questions.watch: “two watchs” — after ch it's “watches”.

questions.prompt: Is your family big?
questions.watch: “four persons” — say “people”.

lessons.title: This / that & my / your
lessons.goal: Point at things near and far, and say who they belong to.

explanation: Use this for something near you, that for something far from you both. Plurals: these (near) and those (far).
Possessive words go before the thing: my, your, his, her. “This is my bag.” “That's your coat.” “Her name is Ana.”
To ask about the owner: “Is this your …?” or “Whose is this?” The answer repeats the owner: “It's mine.” / “No, it's his.”

expressions.meaning: Ask if it belongs to the listener.

lessons.situation: You and the learner arrive early to class and find bags, phones and coats on the tables: identify what's near, what's far, and who owns what.

questions.prompt: Good morning! Is this your bag on the chair?
questions.watch: “Yes, is my bag” — English needs it: “Yes, it's my bag”.

questions.prompt: And this phone? Whose is it?
questions.watch: “It's of Ana” — no of: “It's mine”.

questions.prompt: Look at the board — do you see those words?
questions.watch: “this words” for far things — use “those”.

questions.prompt: I'm holding two keys. Are these your keys?
questions.watch: “this keys” — plural near is “these keys”.

questions.prompt: Is that your bike outside?
questions.watch: Far away: that, not this.

questions.prompt: Whose gloves are those on the floor?
expected: I don't know. They aren't mine.
questions.watch: “They is mine” — plural: “they're mine”.

lessons.title: “Have got”: family
lessons.goal: Say who is in your family and what you have, with have got.

explanation: have got = have. Use it for family, pets and things: “I've got two sisters.” “She's got a dog.” With he/she/it use has got.
Questions flip it: “Have you got any brothers?” Negatives add not: “I haven't got a car.” “He hasn't got time.”
Family words: mother and father (parents), brother, sister, son, daughter, grandmother and grandfather (grandparents). In talk: mum, dad, grandma, grandpa.

examples.text: My parents have got a small dog.

lessons.situation: You swap family photos: describe your family, ask about the learner's, and compare what you both have.

questions.prompt: Tell me about your family — have you got brothers or sisters?
questions.watch: “I have two brother” — plural -s and got: “I've got two brothers”.

questions.prompt: Have you got any pets?
expected: No, I haven't got any pets.
questions.watch: “Have you got some pets?” — questions use any.

questions.prompt: Has your mum got a car?
questions.watch: “Yes, she got” — short answers repeat has.

questions.prompt: Are you the oldest, the youngest or in the middle?
questions.watch: “I am more old” — “the oldest”.

questions.prompt: Have your parents got a garden?
expected: Yes, they have. They've got flowers.
questions.watch: “They has got” — plural takes have.

questions.prompt: I've got a big family — six of us! And you?
questions.watch: “We is five” — “we are five”.

themes.title: The morning rush
themes.subtitle: Against the clock
themes.situation: It's 7:40 and you both have somewhere to be. Describe your morning routine while the clock runs.

themes.title: After work
themes.subtitle: The quiet hours
themes.situation: It's the end of the day. Tell each other what you do in the evening and how you unwind.

lessons.title: Present simple: I / you / we / they
lessons.goal: Talk about routines and facts with I/you/we/they, and ask with do.

explanation: The present simple is for habits and facts: “I work in a bank.” “We live near the park.” With I, you, we and they the verb has no ending.
Questions and negatives use do: “Do you like coffee?” “I don't eat meat.” The main verb goes back to its simple form.
Short answers repeat do: “Do you speak English?” — “Yes, I do.” / “No, I don't.”

expressions.text: Yes, I do. / No, I don't.

lessons.situation: Two neighbours chat in the square about their week: jobs, habits and what they never do.

questions.prompt: So, what do you do?
questions.watch: “What you do?” — questions need do.

questions.prompt: Do you like your job?
questions.watch: “Yes, I like” — short answer is “Yes, I do”.

questions.prompt: Where do you work?
questions.watch: “I work in home” — “from home”.

questions.prompt: Do you speak any other languages?
questions.watch: “I no speak” — “I don't speak”.

questions.prompt: What do you and your friends do at weekends?
questions.watch: “We plays” — with we there's no -s.

questions.prompt: I don't watch much TV. Do you?
questions.watch: Short answers use do, not the verb.

lessons.title: He / she / it + -s & frequency
lessons.goal: Describe another person's routines with the -s ending and say how often things happen.

explanation: With he, she and it the present simple verb takes -s: “She works at night.” “He likes jazz.” This -s is small but very important.
Questions and negatives use does: “Does she live here?” “He doesn't drive.” After does the verb loses its -s: not “Does she works?”
Frequency words say how often: always, usually, often, sometimes, never. They go before the verb: “I always walk to work.” But after be: “He is never late.”

lessons.situation: You catch up about a mutual friend: describe her routines, how often she does things and what she never does.

questions.prompt: Tell me about your best friend — where does she live?
questions.watch: “Where does she lives?” — after does, no -s.

questions.prompt: What does he do at weekends?
questions.watch: “He play” — he needs -s: “He plays”.

questions.prompt: Does she like football?
questions.watch: “Yes, she likes” — short answer: “Yes, she does”.

questions.prompt: How often do you cook?
questions.watch: “I cook two times week” — “twice a week”.

questions.prompt: Is your brother always late?
questions.watch: “He always is late” — after be: “He's always late”.

questions.prompt: My sister never drinks coffee — she hates it. And your family?
questions.watch: “My mum never drink” — keep the -s after never.

lessons.title: Time & daily routine
lessons.goal: Tell the time and describe your day in order.

explanation: Ask with “What time is it?” Answer with o'clock for exact hours: “It's seven o'clock.” For halves say half past: “It's half past seven” (7:30).
Use at for clock times (“at eight”), in the morning/afternoon/evening, and at night.
Order your day with first, then, after that and finally. They make a story out of your routine.

examples.text: I get up at six thirty.
First I shower, then I dress.
Finally, I go to bed at eleven.

expressions.note: Opposite: I go to bed at …

lessons.situation: The learner's first day at a new job: plan the morning together, minute by minute, from waking up to the first meeting.

questions.prompt: Quick — what time is it?
questions.watch: “Is seven o'clock” — statements need it's.

questions.prompt: What time do you get up?
questions.watch: “I get up in seven” — clock times take at.

questions.prompt: Do you have breakfast before or after your shower?
questions.watch: Answer in order: first …, then …

questions.prompt: What do you do in the evening?
questions.watch: “in the night” — evening or “at night”.

questions.prompt: When do you go to bed?
questions.watch: “I go to the bed” — no the: “go to bed”.

questions.prompt: Describe your morning in order — first, then, after that.
expected: First I …, then I …, after that I …
questions.watch: Use the order words — don't list with “and, and, and”.

themes.title: A new neighbourhood
themes.subtitle: Find your way
themes.situation: The learner just moved to the area. Walk the streets together and describe what there is on every corner.

themes.title: Lost in town
themes.subtitle: Ask for help
themes.situation: Your phone died and you are lost. Stop people, ask for directions and follow them.

lessons.title: Can / can't
lessons.goal: Say what you are able to do, ask others for help and give permission.

explanation: can never changes: “I can swim.” “She can swim.” No -s, no to. The negative is can't (or cannot in writing).
Questions flip it: “Can you swim?” For polite requests: “Can you help me?” For permission: “Can I sit here?”
Short answers repeat can: “Yes, I can.” / “No, I can't.”

expressions.note: I can drive, but I can't park!

lessons.situation: You organise a small trip with the learner: who can drive, who can cook, and what you can't do without asking.

questions.prompt: Can you drive?
questions.watch: “Yes, I drive” — repeat can: “Yes, I can”.

questions.prompt: What can you cook?
questions.watch: “I can to cook” — no to after can.

questions.prompt: Can your sister swim?
questions.watch: “She cans swim” — can never takes -s.

questions.prompt: Can I borrow your pen, please?
questions.watch: Answer a request warmly: “Of course”.

questions.prompt: Sorry, can you speak more slowly?
questions.watch: Practise your “Sorry, can you …?” — it opens every repair.

questions.prompt: What's one thing you can't do but want to learn?
expected: I can't <skill>, but I want to learn.
questions.watch: “I can't to play” — no to after can't.

lessons.title: There is / there are
lessons.goal: Say what exists in a place, and ask about it.

explanation: To say something exists, start with there: “There's a pharmacy on the corner.” Singular: there is (there's). Plural: “There are two parks.”
Negatives: “There isn't a lift.” “There aren't any shops.” Questions: “Is there a bank near here?” “Are there any tickets left?”
Say where with prepositions: next to, opposite, behind. “The café is next to the bank.”

examples.text: The bank is opposite the school.

expressions.meaning: Ask for a number of things.

lessons.situation: You show a visitor around the office building: what's on each floor, what's missing, and where exactly things are.

questions.prompt: Is there a supermarket near your flat?
questions.watch: “Is a supermarket?” — start with there.

questions.prompt: How many rooms are there in your home?
questions.watch: “How many rooms has?” — with there: “are there”.

questions.prompt: Is there a lift in the building?
expected: No, there isn't. It's an old building.
questions.watch: “Yes, has lift” — repeat there is.

questions.prompt: What's in your neighbourhood?
questions.watch: One thing → there's; more → there are.

questions.prompt: Are there any good cafés around?
questions.watch: “There aren't some cafés” — negatives take any.

questions.prompt: Where exactly is the pharmacy?
questions.watch: “It's in front the bank” — “opposite” or “in front of”.

lessons.title: Directions & place
lessons.goal: Give and follow simple directions from A to B.

explanation: Start with go straight on, then turn left or turn right. “Go straight on and turn left at the lights.”
Say where the place is: on the left, on the right, on the corner, at the end of the street.
Ask for directions with “How do I get to …?” or “Is it far?” Answers: “Five minutes on foot.”

examples.text: How do I get to the station?
Go straight on for two streets.

expressions.text: on the left / on the right
expressions.note: The pharmacy is on your left.

lessons.situation: The learner's phone has died at a crossroads: ask passers-by for the museum, understand the directions and repeat them back.

questions.prompt: You look lost — can I help?
expected: Yes, please. How do I get to <place>?
questions.watch: Start with “Excuse me” — it buys goodwill.

questions.prompt: OK: go straight on and turn left at the lights. Got it?
expected: Straight on, then left at the lights.
questions.watch: Repeat the route back to check it.

questions.prompt: Is the museum far from here?
questions.watch: “It has five minutes” — “it's five minutes”.

questions.prompt: When you leave, the pharmacy is on your right.
questions.watch: “in the right” — sides take on.

questions.prompt: Where's the nearest metro station?
expected: Go straight on and it's on the corner.
questions.watch: Give order words: straight, then turn.

questions.prompt: Perfect. One last thing — is there a toilet in the museum?
expected: Yes, there is, on the left.
questions.watch: Tie it together: there is + place word.

themes.title: The Sunday market
themes.subtitle: Baskets and barrows
themes.situation: You meet at the Sunday food market: count what's in the baskets, ask what's missing and choose what to cook.

themes.title: Dinner out
themes.subtitle: A table for two
themes.situation: You book and enjoy a dinner out: order dishes, say what you love and hate, and ask for the bill.

lessons.title: Some / any & countables
lessons.goal: Talk about food quantities: what you have, what you need and how much.

explanation: Countable things have a plural: one apple, two apples. Uncountable things have no plural: water, rice, milk, bread.
Use some in affirmative sentences (“We've got some rice”) and any in questions and negatives (“Have we got any milk?” “There isn't any bread.”).
To count uncountables, add a container: a bottle of water, a kilo of rice, a loaf of bread.

examples.text: Can I have a bottle of water?
How much rice do we need?

expressions.meaning: Do we have any…? We don't have any…

expressions.note: How many peppers do we need?

expressions.meaning: Small amounts: a little + uncountable, a few + plural.
expressions.note: a little salt, a few olives

lessons.situation: You cook together from what's in the fridge: list what you have, find out what's missing and write the shopping list.

questions.prompt: Let's cook paella! What have we got?
expected: We've got rice and some tomatoes.
questions.watch: “We've got any rice” — affirmative takes some.

questions.prompt: Do we have any saffron?
questions.watch: “Do we have some…?” — questions prefer any.

questions.prompt: How much rice do we need?
questions.watch: “How many rice?” — rice is uncountable: how much.

questions.prompt: And how many people are coming?
questions.watch: “How much people?” — people is countable here: how many.

questions.prompt: We need milk. Can you get some?
questions.watch: “Yes, I get milk” — confirm the amount: “A litre?”

questions.prompt: We only need a little salt and a few olives.
expected: Got it: a little salt, a few olives.
questions.watch: Countable? a few. Uncountable? a little.

lessons.title: Like / love / hate + -ing
lessons.goal: Talk about what you love, like and hate doing.

explanation: After like, love, hate and don't like, the next verb takes -ing: “I love cooking.” “She hates waiting.”
Questions use do: “Do you like dancing?” Short answers: “Yes, I do.”
To soften, add really or quite: “I really love singing.” “I don't really like getting up early.”

expressions.meaning: Turn the volume up or down.

lessons.situation: You plan a free Sunday together: propose activities and react with love, like, don't mind or hate until you agree on a plan.

questions.prompt: What do you love doing at weekends?
questions.watch: “I love to swim” — with love, -ing is the everyday choice.

questions.prompt: Do you like cooking?
expected: No, I don't. I hate cooking.
questions.watch: “Do you like cook?” — verb+ing after like.

questions.prompt: What's something you hate doing?
questions.watch: “I hate get up” — “hate getting up”.

questions.prompt: Do you mind waiting?
questions.watch: “I don't mind wait” — keep -ing.

questions.prompt: How much do you like films — a bit or a lot?
questions.watch: “I like very much films” — “I really like films”.

questions.prompt: Your friend loves dancing but you don't. What do you say?
expected: I don't like dancing, but thanks!
questions.watch: Soften with really: “I don't really like…”.

lessons.title: Ordering at a café
lessons.goal: Order food and drink, ask for things and pay, in real café English.

explanation: The magic order phrase is “I'd like …” (I would like) — polite and universal. “Can I have …, please?” works everywhere too.
The server asks: “Anything else?” Answer: “That's all, thanks.” Pay with: “The bill, please.”
Choices come fast: “Large or small?” “For here or to go?” Answer with a full mini-sentence: “Small, to go, please.”

examples.text: Can I have a glass of water?
Can I have the bill, please?

lessons.situation: A busy café at breakfast time: order for you and the learner, handle the server's questions and settle the bill.

questions.prompt: Good morning! What can I get you?
questions.watch: “I want a coffee” — understandable, but “I'd like” is politer.

questions.prompt: Anything else?
questions.watch: “Nothing more” — natural is “That's all, thanks”.

questions.prompt: For here or to go?
questions.watch: Answer the part they asked: here/to go.

questions.prompt: Large or small?
questions.watch: “I take large” — “Large, please” is the café norm.

questions.prompt: Here you are — anything else for you two?
questions.watch: “Give me the bill” — “The bill, please” is polite.

questions.prompt: How was everything?
questions.watch: One warm sentence closes the visit.

themes.title: The weekend
themes.subtitle: What happened
themes.situation: Monday catch-up: tell each other what you really did at the weekend, moment by moment.

themes.title: A trip to remember
themes.subtitle: Tell the story
themes.situation: You swap stories of a memorable trip: where you were, what you did and how it ended.

lessons.title: Was / were
lessons.goal: Describe people, places and feelings in the past with was and were.

explanation: Was and were are the past of to be. I/he/she/it → was. You/we/they → were. “I was at home.” “They were at the beach.”
Negatives: wasn't, weren't. Questions flip: “Was it good?” “Where were you?”
Anchor the story in time: yesterday, last night, last week, in 2020, this morning.

expressions.meaning: Give your verdict of the past.

lessons.situation: You bump into a friend who missed the neighbourhood party on Saturday: recount who was there, how it was and what wasn't good.

questions.prompt: Where were you on Saturday?
questions.watch: “I were at home” — with I use was.

questions.prompt: Was the party fun?
questions.watch: “Yes, was fun” — keep it: “Yes, it was”.

questions.prompt: Were there many people?
questions.watch: “There was many” — plural: “there were”.

questions.prompt: How was the music?
questions.watch: “It were good” — it takes was.

questions.prompt: I was so tired on Sunday. And you?
expected: I wasn't tired — I was full of energy.
questions.watch: “I not tired” — past negative: “I wasn't tired”.

questions.prompt: Who was there from your class?
questions.watch: “Who were there” — who takes was here.

lessons.title: Past simple: -ed
lessons.goal: Tell what you and others did, with regular past forms and didn't.

explanation: For finished actions, regular verbs add -ed: work → worked, play → played, watch → watched. The same form works for every person.
Questions and negatives use did + plain verb: “Did you walk?” “I didn't walk.” After did, no -ed: not “Did you walked?”
Spelling: love → loved (no e), study → studied (y→ied), stop → stopped (double p).

expressions.text: Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.

lessons.situation: You compare diaries from a chaotic Tuesday: what you did, what you didn't do, and what the other did first.

questions.prompt: What did you do yesterday evening?
expected: I watched TV and cooked dinner.
questions.watch: “I watch TV” — past answer needs -ed: “I watched”.

questions.prompt: Did you sleep well?
questions.watch: The short answer repeats did: “Yes, I did”.

questions.prompt: Did you walk to work?
questions.watch: “I didn't walked” — after didn't, plain verb.

questions.prompt: What time did you finish work?
questions.watch: “What time did you finished?” — after did, plain finish.

questions.prompt: Did you study English last week?
expected: Yes, I did. I studied on …
questions.watch: “I studyed” — study → studied.

questions.prompt: Your colleague — did she call you?
questions.watch: “Did she called” — after did, plain call.

lessons.title: Your weekend (repaso)
lessons.goal: Tell the story of your weekend in order — past be, past verbs, time anchors — and ask about someone else's.

explanation: A weekend story has three parts: where you were (was/were), what you did (past -ed), and how it was (was + opinion).
Order it with time anchors: on Saturday morning, then, in the evening, later, finally.
Keep the conversation alive: ask back with “What about you?” or “Did you …?”

examples.text: On Friday I was at home — I was exhausted.
On Saturday I visited my parents.
We walked in the park and talked for hours.
In the evening I watched a film.
It was a really good weekend.
What about you? What did you do?

expressions.meaning: Open the story with a time.

lessons.situation: Monday coffee with a friend: take turns telling your weekends, react, and ask at least two questions back.

questions.prompt: So — how was your weekend?
questions.watch: Start with the verdict, then the story.

questions.prompt: What did you do on Saturday?
questions.watch: Use -ed for regular verbs and an order word.

questions.prompt: Were you with friends or alone?
questions.watch: “I was with” — was works with I.

questions.prompt: That sounds nice! Did you eat out?
expected: Yes, we did — we tried a new place.
No, we didn't. We cooked at home.
questions.watch: “Yes, we eat out” — past short answer: “Yes, we did”.

questions.prompt: What about Sunday?
questions.watch: Another time anchor, another scene.

questions.prompt: OK, your turn — ask me about my weekend.
questions.watch: A conversation needs a return serve: ask one question.
